activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Doctors warn against sliding objects like pencils or sticks into a cast to scratch an itch, because they can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining.
story:
The itch started on Tuesday, three days after Lydia broke her arm jumping off the shed roof. It was deep under the cast, in a spot she could not reach, and by Friday it had become the only thing she could think about. She sat at the kitchen table with her homework untouched, flexing her fingers inside the plaster, trying to press her skin against the wall of the cast.

She got up and found a ruler in the drawer. It was thin enough to slide down the gap between her thumb and the cast edge, and she was already lifting her arm to do it when she remembered the doctor's words from the office visit. He had said it plainly: never slide pencils, sticks, or anything like that into a cast to scratch an itch, because it can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining. She had nodded then without really listening. Now she set the ruler down on the table and stared at it.

Her friend Mohamad rang the doorbell that afternoon, holding a bag of sour candies and his own homework. "You look terrible," he said, which was his way of asking how she was.

"There's an itch," Lydia said. "Deep down. It's been going for hours and it's going to drive me insane. I almost used a ruler, but the doctor said not to put sticks in, because you can scrape your skin and wreck the lining." She tapped the cast with her knuckle. "I need another way to hit that spot."

Mohamad tipped his head. "Can air get in there?"

They tried the hairdryer on its cool setting, Mohamad holding the nozzle while Lydia angled her arm. A thin stream of air slid down the gap, and Lydia felt it move along her skin like a cold finger. It reached the itchy patch and the feeling quieted, though it did not vanish entirely. She made him hold it there for a full minute, and when he finally lowered the dryer his arm was trembling from holding it steady, as if he had been serving a heavy tray.

"That actually worked," she said. "It's still there, but it's calmer. Like it went from aggressive to just annoying." She flexed her fingers again. "The itch means the bone is healing, I think. Mom said itching is part of it, so it's a good sign, even if it's the worst good sign ever invented."

"So it has to sustain itself for how many more weeks?" Mohamad asked, unwrapping a candy.

"Five. Five weeks of this." Lydia pulled her sleeve over the cast edge. "Can you come back tomorrow with the hairdryer?"

He held up the sour candy bag. "I'll bring two."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologist Thomas Gordon coined the term 'I-message' in the 1960s: a sentence like 'I felt left out' describes the speaker's feelings instead of blaming the listener with 'you'.
story:
Benjamin sat alone at the end of the lunch table, turning his tray so the pizza wouldn't stare at him. Across the cafeteria, Mohammed was laughing with Rafael about something, probably the rocket they'd promised to build together, the one Benjamin had found out about only because Rafael had left the plans on the lab table with Benjamin's name crossed off the materials list. That stung worse than the pizza.

His dilemma was simple: say nothing and let the friendship rot, or say something wrong and finish the job himself. Last night he'd written a note on a napkin. It started, "You ditched me," which felt satisfying and probably would start a war. He crossed it out. Then he remembered a page from the old counseling booklet Mr. Navarro kept on the shelf behind his desk, the one Benjamin had flipped through while waiting to be excused from gym. A psychologist named Thomas Gordon had come up with something in the 1960s called an "I-message," a sentence that describes the speaker's own feelings instead of blaming the listener with "you." Benjamin hadn't believed a single sentence could matter that much. Now he had a chance to test it.

He wrote slowly, testing the idea like a hypothesis. "You ditched me" got crossed out. "I felt left out when I saw the rocket plans without me" went underneath. It felt invasive at first, like showing everyone the inside of his backpack, but it was his own feeling, not an accusation. He folded the napkin, carried his tray across the room, and stopped at their table.

"Can I sit?" he asked.

Mohammed scooted over without looking up. "Sure. There's room."

Benjamin put the napkin between them. "Read it before you yell at me."

Mohammed read it twice. His ears went pink. "We didn't ditch you. We were going to tell you. Rafael said we should test the fins before the third person got sucked in, because last time you ended up in the hedge."

"The hedge was one time," Benjamin said.

"The hedge had your outline in it," Rafael said. "Like a cartoon."

Mohammed slid the napkin back. "I'm sorry it looked like ditching. I should have just said something."

"Me too. I felt left out," Benjamin said. "That's an I-message, by the way. Gordon, nineteen sixties. It's in Mr. Navarro's booklet, next to the hedge incident, probably."

Mohammed laughed, then tore a piece of napkin and scribbled on it. He held it up: "I promise to preserve one hedge and one best friend." He tucked it into Benjamin's pocket. "Now come look at the fins. You're on parachute duty."

"Parachutes fail," Benjamin said, already following him.

"Not in the hedge they don't."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13, which is why many sites require users to be 13.
story:
Beatrice sat cross-legged on Brynley's bedroom floor with Brynley's phone balanced on her knee, because her own phone was at home charging and this could not wait. The new app everyone at school was using had a green sign-up screen, and it had just asked for her birthday for the third time.

"I put my real birthday," she said. "Twice. It just kicks me back to the start."

Brynley leaned over her shoulder, chewing a strand of her hair. "What did you put?"

"September fourteenth. I turned eleven in September."

"Put thirteen," Brynley said, like it was obvious.

"I'm not lying about my age on the internet." Beatrice said it primly, then immediately felt how prim it sounded, which was ironic, since Brynley's mom had told them both twice not to be on the phone past eight. She tried the real birthday one more time anyway, holding her breath. The screen blinked and showed the same green form, empty again, asking for her date of birth.

"That's not a glitch," she said slowly. "It's doing it on purpose. It only rejects kids under thirteen."

Brynley flopped backward onto her rug. "My cousin says the app hates kids. She's dramatic."

Beatrice turned the phone over in her hands, thinking. Her dad explained internet rules at dinner sometimes, and something was tugging at the back of her memory, a word he had used. Children's something. She typed the phrase into the search bar: websites collecting personal information from children under 13, parental consent. The answer came up before she finished typing. "It's a law," she said. "The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998. Companies have to get parental consent before they collect personal info from kids under thirteen. That's why so many sites say you have to be thirteen. The app isn't being mean. It's following the law."

"So the app is being boring on purpose."

"Basically." Beatrice had a private little flare of pride in her chest, the kind she never showed at school. She had found the rule hiding behind the green screen. But she also understood, in a distant and slightly annoying way, that knowing the rule did not change the rule. She was eleven until September, and September was a long way off.

Brynley sat up. "So just wait? That's your big solution?"

"No." Beatrice scrolled to the bottom of the sign-up page and found a small link that said parental consent options. She clicked it. There was a form a parent could fill out, with permission and a signature. She turned the phone toward Brynley. "Can I ask your mom to call my dad?"

"You want to document permission. Like a permission slip for the internet."

"It's kind of a concept, isn't it? Permission slips for everything." Beatrice was already composing the text to her father in her head, deciding which words sounded the most responsible. She typed out the first line, showed it to Brynley for approval, and pressed send.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Keith Johnstone's 1979 book 'Impro' taught that characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama.
story:
Avery had never set foot in the dilapidated community theatre before Tuesday, and now she was there four afternoons a week, rehearsing for the summer showcase. Mr. Perera supervised the rehearsals from a folding chair in the third row, calling out notes while the kids worked through their scenes. Avery's scene kept dying. Every time Graydon offered her something, like "Quick, the dragon is coming," she answered with "No, there's no dragon," and the scene fell flat like a dropped curtain.

"Say yes, and add something," Mr. Perera called. "That's the whole game."

That part she could fix. The harder problem was that even when she said yes, her scenes with Graydon still felt like two people reading a cereal box. On Thursday, hunting for a prop crown in the dusty storeroom, she found a battered paperback taped shut with a note folded inside the back cover. The note read: "To whoever finds this: the answer is in chapter five. High or low, the shift is the engine. Trust it. Signed, a kid who was terrified here in 1986." The book was Impro, by Keith Johnstone, 1979, and the margins were full of someone's pencil scribbles.

Avery read the chapter twice on the bus. Characters in a scene played higher or lower status, the book said, and shifting status created drama. That was the hidden pattern she'd been missing, and she had an idea for testing it. At Friday's rehearsal, she and Graydon ran the scene Larissa had written for them, a king and a servant. Avery played the king, ordering Graydon around, and the scene limped along, safe and boring. Then, on her next line, she flipped it. "Fetch my soup," she said, and then she lowered her eyes. "Unless... you think I should get it myself."

Graydon blinked, straightened up, and pointed at her. "Yes. You should get it yourself. And my laundry too."

Larissa laughed so hard from the front row that she slid off her seat, and Mr. Perera leaned forward in his chair for the first time all week. The scene got funnier the more orders the servant gave, because the king kept shrinking while the servant kept growing. Avery felt the insight land in her bones: the shift was the engine, just like the note said.

Afterward she found Graydon alone by the water fountain, staring at his shoes. "I was scared," he admitted. "Being the boss up there, that actually helped." She handed him the old paperback. "Chapter five," she said. "Keep it till Tuesday."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In a 1977 study, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true.
story:
Ms. Ahmed had put a stack of old magazine ads on the history classroom table and told the class to sort them into piles. "One pile for ads that use famous people," she said, walking between the desks. "One for ads that use loaded words. One for ads that try to convince you everyone is buying the thing. I'll be around to supervise, but I want your own ideas first."

Luca picked up a faded ad from 1978. A television star stood beside a cassette player, grinning. "Celebrity testimonial," he said, and dropped it on the first pile. Haley held up another one. "This one says 'the car everyone trusts.' That's the everyone pile, right?" Malik read a shampoo ad aloud. "'The amazing, luxurious formula for gorgeous hair.' Those are the loaded words. They sound great but they don't actually say anything."

"They're tricks," Malik said.

"Not tricks exactly," Ms. Ahmed said. "More like techniques. People who write these know how our minds work."

Luca's family wanted a new television, and his mother kept saying she'd buy the brand "everybody knows is the best." Luca had asked her how she knew, and she'd said she just knew, that she'd heard it again and again. He wanted to figure out whether that was a real reason or not, because the other brand cost sixty dollars less.

He remembered the ads lesson and thought about it on the walk home. His mother had never compared the two televisions. She had never read a review. She had only heard one claim over and over, at the salon, from his uncle, from a commercial.

The next day he tried something. In class, before the bell, he told Haley, "A duck can't see the color blue." It wasn't true; he'd made it up the night before. At lunch he told Malik the same thing. He said it to Haley's cousin after school, and to his neighbor, and then once more to Malik on Friday. Each time he said it in the same flat way, no proof.

Monday, Haley said, "You know how ducks can't see blue? Malik told me too."

"I know," Malik said. "I heard it from Haley's cousin. It must be true."

"Did anyone show you anything?" Luca asked. "Like an actual fact about duck eyes?"

They both shook their heads.

"So you believe it because you heard it, what, five times?"

"It just seems true," Malik said. "It rings a bell."

Luca went home and did some searching on the library computer. He found exactly what he was looking for. In 1977, a researcher named Lynn Hasher and her colleagues had run a study, and the people in it rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing the statements repeated, whether or not the statements were true. Repetition alone did the work. That was the whole factor, hearing something over and over, and it didn't care if the something was real.

On Tuesday he brought the printout to class. "Ms. Ahmed, this connects to the ads. The 'everybody's buying it' ads, and the ones with the famous actor. They repeat the same claim everywhere so it starts feeling true."

Ms. Ahmed read the page. "The Hasher study. Good find."

"That's why my mom thinks one television is the best," Luca said. "It's not an authentic opinion from testing them. It's repetition. She heard it five times, so it feels like a fact."

He brought the printout home and put it next to the sixty-dollars-cheaper television ad on the kitchen counter.

His mother picked it up while the pasta water was boiling. "What's this?"

"That's the 1977 study," Luca said. "Read the last line out loud."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Confirmation bias is the tendency to accept claims that fit what we already believe and to doubt claims that do not, without checking either.
story:
Simon had ten minutes before the library closed, and he meant to spend all of them proving Kieran wrong.

"You're writing your article on the Tigers game?" Simon had asked at lunch, and Kieran had grinned. "Then you should put in that the Falcons' coach got suspended for cheating. Everybody's saying it."

"Who's everybody?" Simon had asked, but Kieran had just shrugged and gone back to his sandwich. That was two days ago, and Simon's article was due Friday. He spread his notes across the library table: the score sheet from Saturday's game, a printout of the league standings, and his laptop with the league website open. Nothing he could find mentioned any suspension.

Madilyn slid into the chair across from him, balancing a stack of books she had no intention of checking out. "Still hunting the ghost coach?" she said.

"It's not a ghost if it's real," Simon said. "It's a claim. It can be checked. That's the whole difference between it and Kieran saying the Tigers have ugly uniforms. That's just his opinion. Nobody can look up ugly."

Madilyn snickered. "So look it up."

"I'm trying. The league site has a news page, and there's nothing there. No suspension, no fine, nothing."

He typed the coach's name into the search bar and hit enter. The only results were three years of box scores and one photo from a fundraiser. Simon sat back. Maybe the story had come from somewhere older, something he hadn't found yet, buried deep in an archive. He walked to the reference desk, where Mr. Xu was reshelving returns.

"Is there a way to search old league records?" Simon asked. "Like from before the website?"

Mr. Xu considered him over his glasses. "The library keeps the local papers on microfilm, but those go back decades. Are you sure you need to go that far?"

Simon wasn't sure of anything anymore. He budgeted his last minutes carefully: five for the microfilm machine, he decided, and three to get back and write. The reels whirred under his hands, and the pages slid past in gray sheets. He slowed at anything with the word Falcons. A bake sale. A field renovation. A profile of the league's founders, who built the whole program on a shoestring budget and refused anything extravagant, not even a scoreboard. No suspension anywhere.

Then he found it. A letter to the editor from three years back, complaining that referees favored the Falcons. The paper had printed a correction two weeks later, because a reporter had actually checked the penalty counts. The Falcons had the median number of penalties in the league, right in the middle. The letter writer had just repeated what fans liked to believe.

Simon read the correction twice, and the pieces slid together in his head. He walked back to his table slowly, letting the thought finish forming.

"Madilyn," he said, "I know why the story spread. Kieran wants the Tigers to be the good guys, so a story about the Falcons cheating sounds right to him. He never checked it, because it fit what he already believed. It's called confirmation bias. And everyone who passed it on did the same thing."

"So it's fake?"

"It's unverified," Simon said, and started typing. "There's a difference."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The parable of the blind men and the elephant, from ancient India, describes people who each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it completely differently.
story:
Ms. Choi wrote one word on the board, "Perspective," and then asked the class to describe the mural project the art club had been working on for three weeks. Ruby raised her hand first. "It's a desert," she said. "All sand and a desolate canyon, because that's my panel."

"That's not what it is at all," said Samantha, two rows over. "It's a garden. My panel has a fountain and a lemon tree." Brixton shook his head. "You're both wrong. It's a night sky. I painted stars over my whole section." The three of them started talking over each other, and Ruby felt her ears go hot. They had each spent every Tuesday after school on their own corner of the long wall in the gym hallway, and it seemed impossible that they were describing the same mural.

Ms. Choi held up a hand. "Interesting," she said, and nothing more, which was her way of making everybody wait. Then she asked Samantha to fetch something from the supply cabinet. Samantha came back with a photocopy of an old story and handed copies down the rows.

Ruby read it quickly. It was a parable from ancient India, the sheet said, about blind men and an elephant. Each man touched a different part of the elephant, so one, feeling the trunk, said the elephant was like a thick snake, and another, feeling the leg, said it was like a pillar, and the man at the ear said it was like a fan, and the one at the tail said it was like a rope. They argued about it, each certain, because each had touched only one part.

"That's us," Brixton said, not even waiting to be called on. "We've only seen our own panels." Ruby looked at the paper again. She had been so sure the mural was a desert that she had never once walked down the hallway to look at the rest of it. Neither, apparently, had anyone else.

Ruby had an idea she wanted to verify. She asked if they could leave the classroom for five minutes, and Ms. Choi nodded. The three of them walked to the gym hallway and stood at the far end of the wall, where none of them had stood before. From there the mural opened up all at once: Samantha's garden sat right at the edge of Ruby's desert, as if an oasis had bloomed there, and Brixton's night sky stretched above both, its stars reflected in the fountain.

"It's a journey," Ruby said slowly. "Day to night. Desert to garden." Samantha frowned at the wall, then tilted her head. "I spent all that time on one lemon tree and I never knew it was at the end of a journey," she said. "I thought you two were just doing backgrounds." She paused. "I changed my mind about the whole thing. I like it better now."

That evening Ruby wrote a note to her grandfather, who had asked her at dinner what she was building at school. "We made a mural," she wrote, "and for three weeks I only knew my own piece of it. There's a story from ancient India about blind men who each touch one part of an elephant and describe it completely differently, and that was us, except we could see. It took walking to the end of the hall to fix it." She sealed the envelope, set it by the door for the morning post, and turned out the light.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution says no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves.
story:
Simon had heard the phrase "I plead the Fifth" three times in one episode of the detective show, and by the third time he was leaning toward the screen with his chin in his hands, wondering what a fifth could possibly be. He asked Tayla about it at the community centre on Saturday, where they were supposed to be working on their civics project in the big room with the squeaky floor.

"It means you don't have to answer," Tayla said, stacking her note cards. "My uncle says it all the time when my aunt asks who ate the last cookie."

"But a fifth of what?" Simon pulled out his phone. In the copy of the US Constitution Ms. Han had lent him, he found the Fifth Amendment and read it slowly, twice. "It says no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves." He looked up. "That's it? That's the whole thing people say on TV?"

Calum wandered over from the ping pong table, still holding a paddle. "Ms. Han is going to nominate people to explain an amendment out loud next week," he said. "She told me she's picking whoever can put it in their own words. Whoever, meaning not me."

Simon read the amendment aloud one more time, then folded his arms and stared at the far wall. "Okay, so here's a test. Tayla, you're a detective. You think I broke the vending machine. Can you make me testify against myself?"

Tayla sat up straighter and pointed at him. "Tell us exactly where you were when the glass cracked."

"No person can be forced," Simon said, grinning, "in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves. So I can just not answer. Even if I'm guilty, even if I'm innocent, I can stay quiet."

Calum tapped the paddle against his leg. "Wait, so it protects guilty people?"

"It protects everybody," Simon said. He paused, because he wasn't sure that was right, so he went back to the page and read the line again. "It says person. Not innocent person. Just person."

Ms. Han came in carrying a box of markers, her eccentric purple hat with the felt stars bobbing as she walked. She paused near their table. "I hear someone reciting amendments."

"I can explain one," Simon said. "The principle is that the government can't make you testify against yourself in a criminal case. That's the Fifth Amendment."

Ms. Han raised an eyebrow above her glasses. "In your own words, then. As if I knew nothing."

Simon took a breath. "If you're on trial for a crime, nobody can force you to give evidence that would make you look guilty. You can refuse. On TV they say 'I plead the Fifth' because that's the amendment it comes from."

"Interesting," Ms. Han said, and wrote something in her notebook. Calum leaned over Simon's shoulder. "So next Saturday, you nominate me for hardest amendment, right?"

"Calum," Simon said, "you can't nominate yourself. I checked."

Tayla laughed so hard she knocked over her note cards, and Simon started stacking them for her, still grinning.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
story:
The bus lurched around the corner by the pond, and Livia slid across the vinyl seat into Eliam, who was already holding his phone like it owed him money. "Trade deadline's at eight tonight," he said. "You have to pick. Kolton wants Ramirez, and I'm starting to think he's right."

Livia shook her head. "Ramirez is ranked fourth in the whole league. Fourth. You don't trade away the fourth-ranked player." Kolton, one row back, leaned over the seat like a predatory seagull hovering over someone's french fries. "Rankings are one number," he said. "You keep saying fourth like it's a law of nature."

"Then give me a better number," Livia said.

Kolton grinned. "Give me until the school parking lot." For the next ten minutes he was quiet, which was so unusual that the kid across the aisle asked if he was sick. Livia watched fields go by and worried. Her fantasy team was her one good thing this fall, and she'd spent two weeks protecting it while her math grade sat on a plateau, stubbornly stuck at a C no matter how many quizzes she retook.

As the bus squealed to its second stop, Eliam held up his phone. "Okay, so last night my uncle took me to the sports bar, and he told me this story. There's a book called Moneyball, came out in 2003, by Michael Lewis." He scrolled through his notes, which he had actually typed up, because that was Eliam. "It's about how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players."

"On-base what?" Livia said.

"On-base percentage," Eliam said. "My uncle says the whole book is about it."

"Okay, but what does that have to do with Ramirez?" Livia asked, though a small electric feeling had started in her stomach, the same one she got when a math problem suddenly flipped from impossible to obvious.

Kolton leaned forward again. "Think about it. A ranking squishes everything into one number. It doesn't tell you how the guy got there. I pulled both their game logs. Ramirez is ranked high because of three huge games back in April. Since June he's been walking maybe once a week and swinging at everything. The other guy, Prasad, nobody ranks him, but he gets on base constantly. He's cheap because everyone's looking at the ranking."

Livia stole Eliam's phone and checked, because checking was how she did everything. Kolton was right. April had been spectacular, and everything after had been ordinary. The single ranking number could summarize the whole season, sure, but it summarized it the way a photograph summarizes a year: one frozen moment, three good games doing all the work. Meanwhile Prasad's boring, steady numbers piled up underneath the ranking like coins under a couch cushion.

"So Oakland, they had no money," she said slowly, working it out as the bus pulled through the school gate. "They found players everybody else ignored, because everybody was staring at the famous numbers, and the A's looked at the ones that actually told you who gets on base."

"Boom," said Kolton.

Eliam checked the time. "Deadline's tonight at eight, not now. You can sit with it."

"I don't need to sit with it," Livia said, and typed the trade offer right there, jostled between two eighth graders and a backpack full of math homework she now planned to actually do. "Prasad for Ramirez. If my grade can get off its plateau, so can my team."

The bus hissed to a stop. Kolton stood up in the aisle and pointed at her like a game-show host. "The Livia Athletics," he announced, "small budget, big brain."

"Get off the bus before it leaves with you on it," Livia said.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Muscle soreness after an unfamiliar workout is usually worst 24 to 72 hours afterward, which is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
Ellie had felt great walking out of the gym on Monday, so great that she'd told Johan the tryouts were nothing to fear. Now it was Tuesday, and she was gripping the stair rail outside the gymnasium, lowering herself one step at a time while her thighs burned like someone had filled them with sand. Johan hauled the door open for her, wincing as he did it. "You too?" he asked. "I could barely get out of bed." Inside, kids who had sprinted freely yesterday were limping and rubbing their arms, and Gregoire sat on the lowest bleacher, staring at his own legs as if they belonged to a stranger.

Ellie lowered herself onto the bench beside him. "Here's the thing that's bugging me," she said. "We were fine last night. Fine. And the workout was Monday. So why is it worse now, the day after, instead of right after?" She'd been turning it over since dawn, when her calves had announced themselves before her alarm did. Gregoire pulled out his phone, thumbed through something his mom had sent him, and held it up. "My mom's a nurse. She says it's called delayed onset muscle soreness," he read. "She says it's usually worst 24 to 72 hours after." Ellie counted backward on her fingers. Monday's workout plus one day was today. That meant tomorrow might be just as bad, and maybe even the day after that, which raised a problem she hadn't considered.

"Mr. García said cuts happen Thursday," she said. "So we're going to be at our most wrecked right when it matters." She looked across the gym at the coach, who stood near the racks of balls with the calm of someone who had seen all this before, and she could not articulate why that calm bothered her. She formed a plan and tested it out loud: "If yesterday was hardest on our legs, maybe today we go full speed anyway. It already happened to us. Hiding in the corner won't make Thursday less sore." Johan frowned, but he stood up when she did, and Gregoire followed, moving like a man twice his age.

The warm-up was misery, but midway through layups Ellie noticed something: the ache didn't vanish, exactly, but it loosened, and her shots stopped clanging off an indifferent rim. She found an economy in her movements that she hadn't had on Monday, no wasted steps, just cut, plant, release. Mr. García watched her for a long moment and wrote something on his clipboard.

Thursday, the list went up. Ellie's name was on it, third from the top, and so was Johan's. Gregoire's was not. She was still staring at his missing name when Gregoire laughed and admitted the twist himself: he had skipped half of Monday's drills to save his legs, then done a secret solo workout Monday night, thinking it would give him an edge. "So my worst soreness hit Wednesday," he said, "right when he was watching, and I played like a scarecrow." Ellie thought about her own choice, going full speed on the sore day, and about whether Gregoire's cleverness had been smarter all along, only timed badly. She couldn't decide, and she didn't try very hard to. "Open gym starts Monday," she said, handing him her water bottle. "Come on. Day one hurts less if you're already sore."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In experiments by psychologist Henri Tajfel, people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random.
story:
The banner over the community centre door said Community Day, but inside it felt more like a contest waiting to happen. Taylor had signed up for the afternoon workshop because Freyja had begged her to, and because last summer she had made a mistake she still turned over at night: she had ditched her cabin at the talent show to sit with the older kids, and her cabin had stopped talking to her for the rest of the week. She wanted to understand how groups got that way, so fast.

Mr. Hernández, who ran the centre, stood on a chair with a coffee can. "Everybody draw a slip," he called out. "Red band or blue band. That's your team for the scavenger hunt." Taylor pulled a red slip, and so did a boy named Mahmoud, who grinned at her like they'd known each other for years. They had met four minutes ago.

The hunt sent them through the gym, the art room, and the kitchen, where a parent handed out clue cards. By the second clue, Taylor noticed the reds were already chanting something about crushing blue, and the blues were hissing back across the hallway. She decided to monitor it, the way her science teacher had shown them for the plant experiment: watch, write down, don't interfere. Every time someone cheered for their own band and booed the other, she marked a tally in her notebook. The count climbed like a temperature.

"Nobody even knows each other," she said to Mahmoud while they searched behind the bleachers for a plastic coin. "The bands came out of a coffee can."

"Feels like they matter anyway," Mahmoud said. He had told her earlier that his family had moved here from Egypt three years ago, and that at his old school nobody sat with him until spring. "When I first got here, I'd have joined any group that would have me."

That was the piece she'd been missing. Later, when the reds won and somebody yelled that blues were losers, Taylor stood on the stage steps and read out her tallies. "Mr. Hernández picked these teams out of a can. Random, like flipping a coin. And I counted thirty-one times we cheered for reds and booed blues in one hour."

A blue girl in the front frowned. "So we're rivals over nothing?"

"There was a psychologist, Tajfel," Taylor said, because Freyja had found it on the centre's library tablet that afternoon. "He did experiments where the groups were assigned completely at random, and people still favoured their own group."

The room went quiet, in a gradual way, like the buzz of the vending machine fading. A boy took off his red band and folded it into his pocket. Then Freyja stood up on a chair and held out her blue band toward the red team.

"Trade you," she said.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
story:
Arianna had eleven minutes to finish the hallway bulletin board before first bell, and the paper letters kept curling off the wall like they wanted to escape. The board was for the school news team, and her job was the headline: "Poll Shows Support for New Gym Jumps 10 Points." She had the poll data in her hand, a coffee-stained printout from Ms. Silva's class.

Chelsey hurried over with her ponytail half undone, holding her phone. "Okay, problem. The town website says support went up 25 percent. The Gazette says 10. They're talking about the same poll, Arianna. Same poll, different numbers. Which one is lying?"

"Neither one is lying, probably," Arianna said, pressing down a letter S that popped back up at her. She checked the printout. Forty percent of people wanted the new gym last spring. Fifty percent wanted it now.

Oceanne appeared beside them, chewing the end of a pen. "Ten and twenty-five can't both describe the same change. That's not how numbers work."

Arianna stared at the two figures, 40 and 50, and turned them over in her head the way she turned over a Rubik's cube before making a move. Then she said, slowly, "Wait. It went from 40 to 50. So it's ten percentage points higher. But 50 is 25 percent bigger than 40." She said it out loud twice, testing it, the way you test a wobbly shelf by pushing on it.

"Both stories are true?" Chelsey said. "Both? At once?"

"Ten points. Twenty-five percent. Same change," Arianna said. "One paper counted the points, the other counted the percent."

Oceanne dropped her pen. "So the Gazette's ranking of 'most misleading headline of the week' is itself misleading. That's almost prestigious levels of irony."

Five minutes to bell. The letters were still curling, and the whole board looked like it had been assembled by a nervous algorithm with a grudge against adhesives. Chelsey read the finished headline and frowned. "People will think 10 and 25 are different changes. We could get letters."

Arianna considered a compromise: put both numbers on the board, with the words "same thing" in between. She found the extra letters in the box, mostly bent Ys and a single dusty Q. There was no second percent sign anywhere, so she cut one out of red construction paper with the classroom scissors, and it came out slightly crooked, like a small drunk tree.

The bell rang as she pressed the last letter flat with her thumb, holding it there, counting silently to ten, feeling the paper's warmth and hoping the tape would compromise with the wall.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Historians still do not know who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775; British and colonial witnesses each said the other side fired first.
story:
Isabella had one job at her grandmother's seventieth birthday party: keep her little cousins away from the cake table until the candles were lit. It should have been easy, except that Uncle Ray and Great-Aunt Pearl were arguing in the corner, and she could not stop listening.

"That shot came from the British line, Pearl. I've read the reports."

"Reports written by whom?" Aunt Pearl tapped her cane. "Our people were there. Every colonial witness said the redcoats fired first."

Isabella drifted closer, pretending to straighten the napkins. She had a history test on the Revolution coming up, and this sounded exactly like something Ms. Menon would put on it. Uncle Ray was recounting the morning of April 1775 at Lexington, how the two sides stood facing each other in the gray light, and how nobody, even now, knows who fired the first shot. "The British witnesses swore the colonials fired first," he said. "The colonial witnesses swore the opposite. Historians still argue about it."

"Ridiculous," Aunt Pearl said. "Someone must have seen it."

"Everyone saw it," Uncle Ray said. "They just saw it differently."

A cousin tugged Isabella's sleeve, and she nearly missed it. Aunt Pearl was frowning now, not angry, thinking. "You know, my mother told that story her way for sixty years," she said slowly. "I always thought she was just being stubborn." She paused. "Maybe she believed it completely. Maybe they all did."

Isabella's mind was racing. People standing on opposite sides of the same road, hearing the same crack of a musket, and each side certain it came from the other. She wanted to test it. At the dessert table she took two paper cups, whispered something different into each, and gave one to her cousin Victor and one to her classmate Kingsley, who had arrived with his parents five minutes earlier. "Both of you go stand by the front window and close your eyes," she said. "Then tell me exactly what you hear."

They stood at the window while she, from the kitchen doorway, dropped a metal spoon onto the tile floor. The clatter was sharp and unmistakable.

"Someone in the kitchen dropped something," Kingsley said, eyes still shut.

"Something fell outside," Victor said. "On the porch. It came from behind me."

Isabella opened her mouth, then closed it. Same spoon, same clatter, two different directions, and both boys sounded completely sure. She felt a small chill, the kind that comes when something you learned suddenly becomes real.

"Well?" Kingsley demanded.

"Your verdicts don't match," she said, "and you were both wrong and both right." She held up the spoon. "That's my whole history essay, right there."

From the corner, Aunt Pearl raised her teacup toward her. "Now you understand your great-grandmother," she called across the tranquil, candlelit room. "Hurry up and light the cake before the cousins get it."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: Freytag's pyramid, based on Gustav Freytag's 1863 book on drama, pictures a plot as rising to the climax at its peak and then falling.
story:
Jeremy had read his story four times, and something about it was wrong, but he could not say what. He sat at the back table of the school library with his draft in front of him, a tale about a smuggler who sneaks past a harbor tariff by hiding silver inside barrels of fish. Mario leaned over from the next chair, chewing his pencil.

"Your dialogue looks weird," Mario said. "You put the period outside the quotation marks. Twice."

Jeremy calibrated the distance between his comma and the closing quotation mark, sliding his pencil eraser along the line like a tiny gauge, and fixed the first one. The second one he left, because he was not sure the rule held for a question mark. But the punctuation was small trouble. The big trouble was that his story felt flat, like a hallway with no door at the end, and Mr. Torres was collecting drafts in fifteen minutes.

Then Valerie sat down across from him and flipped her worksheet over. On the blank back she had drawn a mountain, wide at the base, sharp at the top, sloping down the other side. She tapped the peak with her pen. "It's called Freytag's pyramid," she said. "It's based on Gustav Freytag's 1863 book on drama." She traced her finger up the slope. "The plot rises to the climax at the peak, then falls."

Jeremy stared at the drawing. His smuggler story, he realized, climbed steadily and then just stopped, like a hiker who reaches the top and finds nothing there. He grabbed a fresh sheet and counted his scenes. The harbor inspection, the false manifest, the informer's warning, all of it rose in a straight line with no peak at all. He had scattered the tension evenly, thinking that was the same as building it.

He crossed out his ending and wrote a new one, slowly now, his hand almost shaking. The inspector's hand hovered over the third barrel, the one with the silver. The smuggler's little brother, who had been quiet for two pages, stepped forward and lied. Every line of dialogue, he checked twice, commas tucked inside the marks, the question mark inside too, because he had decided to test it and it looked right. The room seemed to hold still while he wrote the final paragraph, the one where the brother confesses on the dock.

Mr. Torres walked between the tables collecting pages. When he reached Jeremy, he read the last half of the page standing there, and his eyebrows went up.

"Who told you to put the lie at the peak?" he asked.

Jeremy slid Valerie's worksheet across the table, mountain side up, and pointed at the summit. "She drew me a map," he said.

"He built the climb himself," Valerie said. "I only gave him the mountain."

Mr. Torres marked the top of the drawing with a small check and moved on. Jeremy looked at the peak, then at his own last line, still wet enough to smear, and held the page flat with both hands until it dried.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Knowing a word's language of origin can help with spelling: the 'k' sound in 'chorus' is spelled 'ch' because it comes from Greek, while the 'sh' in 'chef' comes from French.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and popcorn, and the folding chairs were packed with students from every homeroom. Jade sat on the stage between Athena and a boy from another class, clutching her word list so tightly the paper felt like it might tear. For two weeks she had studied every evening, and she had noticed something odd: "chef" and "chorus" both started with a sound like "ch," but the letters after it were different. She had written them side by side a dozen times, and the difference nagged at her like a loose tooth.

"Chorus," said Ms. Bautista, reading from the judge's card. "The language of origin is Greek."

Jade's mind spun. She remembered the dictionary entry she'd stared at the night before. "Chef" had come from French, and its "sh" sound was spelled "c-h." "Chorus" came from Greek. If the origin made a difference, then maybe in a Greek word the "k" sound would be spelled "c-h" too. It was a guess, but a testable one, the same principle she used in science class: change one thing, watch what happens. She asked for the word again, drew the letters in the air with her finger, and said, "C-H-O-R-U-S. Chorus."

"Correct," said Ms. Bautista, and the sound of it seemed to propel Jade straight out of her chair. Athena, waiting in line for her own turn, gave her a double thumbs-up.

Round after round, the field shrank. Athena went out on "rhythm" and shrugged it off, mouthing "you've got this" from the second row of chairs. The boy beside Jade misspelled "bureau" and walked off stage with his shoulders slumped but his head up, because his coach patted his back and whispered something that made him grin.

Then there were two: Jade and a seventh grader with an elastic headband who chewed her lip before every word. Ms. Bautista looked at the card and paused longer than usual. "Chef," she said. "The language of origin is French."

Jade almost laughed out loud. The twist she needed had landed right in her lap. The word that had started her whole investigation, the one whose "sh" sound had puzzled her for two weeks, was now the final word of the bee. French, she thought, so the "sh" sound is spelled "c-h," just like in the dictionary entry. She said it slowly, letter by letter, and the gymnasium went silent until the last syllable hung in the air.

"Correct," said Ms. Bautista, "and that makes our champion." Athena vaulted onto the stage before the applause even started, and Monica waved both arms from the third row. The trophy was small and slightly crooked, but Jade held it up anyway. "Chef," she said to Athena. "Two weeks of my life, and it comes down to soup."

"Best soup ever," Athena said, and hugged her so hard the trophy wobbled.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12 and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers aged 13 to 18.
story:
Joshua slumped onto the plastic chair by the pharmacy counter, waiting while the pharmacist filled his mom's prescription. His stomach had been knotted all morning, his hands were cold, and he had snapped at Naomie on the bus for no reason he could name. He felt like something invisible was squeezing him, and he wanted to find out what it was. Behind the counter, Mr. Halvorsen, who also lived three houses down, counted pale pills into an orange bottle.

A poster on the wall caught Joshua's eye. It showed a sleeping kid and a row of numbers. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommended 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12, and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers aged 13 to 18. Joshua did the math on his fingers. He had been gaming until midnight every night that week, then waking at seven for school. Seven hours. He was twelve, so he was supposed to get 9 to 12 hours, and he was two hours short of even the bottom of that range, every single night. Maybe the squeezing feeling had a cause he could not see but could count.

"Mr. Halvorsen," he said when the pharmacist slid the bag across the counter, "does not sleeping enough make you feel weird? Like your stomach's in a knot?" Mr. Halvorsen nodded. "Sounds like stress. Your body sends signals. Slow breathing tells it to stand down." He showed Joshua how to breathe in for four counts and out for six, right there between the cough syrup and the waiting chairs. Joshua felt slightly ridiculous, a civilian doing drills in the middle of a store, but the knot loosened a little.

At school, Joshua told Everett his plan: in bed by ten, phone in the kitchen, four-count breathing before lights out. "That's not going to work," Everett said. "Sleep is sleep. My cousin stays up till two and he's fine." Joshua shrugged. "Then I'll test it for a week and see." Naomie offered to supervise the experiment, which mostly meant texting him "BREATHE" at 9:55 every night and asking each morning to rate his day from one to ten.

The week had its bumps. On Tuesday he forgot the phone rule and lost an hour; on Wednesday he was so tired he snapped again and had to apologize to Naomie. But by Friday the mornings had changed. His hands were warm, his stomach was quiet, and when Mr. Halvorsen came into his dad's hardware store to buy a molten-metal-looking door hinge for his workshop, Joshua reported, "Nine and a half hours. Best score yet." Even Everett, who had watched the whole thing, changed his mind and admitted he wanted to try the schedule himself, because his own mornings were terrible in exactly the way Joshua's used to be.

"It's like an experiment you run on yourself," Everett said, pulling out his phone to set a bedtime alarm. Joshua grinned and showed him the breathing count on his fingers, four in, six out, while Naomie pretended to check her watch. "9:55, boys," she said. "Breathe."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A heritage language is one spoken at home or in the family that differs from the main language of the wider community, and heritage speakers may speak it without reading it.
story:
Kate had one job at Kaleb's birthday party: coordinate the games, the cake, and the piñata so nothing collided with his grandmother's visit at four o'clock. She had a clipboard and everything. What she did not have a plan for was the moment Kaleb's grandmother handed him a card, and Kaleb's smile went stiff.

His grandmother chattered away in what Kate guessed was Portuguese, and Kaleb answered easily, laughing, arguing about whether she had made too much food. Then he opened the card, and his eyes stopped moving. He held it at a diagonal, tilted it toward the window, as if the words might rearrange themselves in better light. Steam from the kitchen drifted past him like vapor rising off a pot, and he just stood there.

"That's from my vovó," said his cousin Byron, leaning over Kate's shoulder. "She writes in Portuguese. Kaleb talks it fine but can't read a word of it. He's a heritage speaker." Byron shrugged. "It's what you call it when you speak a language from home but never learned to read it."

Kate filed that away, because she had a bigger problem: the card was clearly the good part of the present, and Kaleb was now hiding it behind the cake box. She tried an experiment. She slid the card out, pointed at the first line, and said to Kaleb, "Read it out loud. Just sound it out."

"I can't read it," Kaleb said, ears going pink. "I can say anything you say, though."

So Kate had an idea. She carried the card to his grandmother, and Kaleb's grandmother read it aloud, slow and dramatic, tapping each word with one finger. Kaleb repeated every line right behind her, matching her rhythm, and somewhere in the middle his voice wobbled because the card said he was her favorite person to argue with, and that she was proud of him even when he ate all the pão de queijo before everyone else arrived.

"Aha," Kaleb said, wiping his eye with his wrist and pretending he wasn't. "So the trick is, you read it and I echo it. Like a duet."

"That's cheating," said Byron.

"That's engineering," said Kaleb.

His grandmother tapped the last line and raised her eyebrows at Kate. "Now her," she said to Kaleb. "She reads English. You teach her to say one word back to me."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: The hottest weeks usually come several weeks after the summer solstice, because land and oceans take time to warm up.
story:
Jasmine pushed the flashlight closer to the basketball in the middle of the lawn. "Okay, pretend this is Earth. The broom handle through it is the axis."

Salma crouched down beside her. "Why is it leaning sideways instead of straight up?"

"Because Earth's axis is tilted," Jasmine said. "That's the whole point. It stays tilted the same way while Earth goes around the sun, so different parts lean toward the light at different times of year."

Cash spun the basketball slowly, one finger on each side of the broom handle. "Hold on. When we lean toward the sun, that's summer?"

"Right. The light hits us more directly," Jasmine said. "Watch." She shone the flashlight straight down on the top half of the ball and traced the bright patch with chalk on the grass. Then she tilted the handle so the same spot angled away, and the light spread out thin and pale across a much bigger area. "Same amount of energy, but spread out. That's winter light."

Cash pulled out his notebook. "I'm supposed to document every step for the project. Ms. Kapoor said our demonstration is due first period tomorrow, so we'd better get this right."

Jasmine sat back on her heels and frowned at the chalk circle. "There's one part I keep getting wrong. Last summer I did a whole chart. I wrote down the temperature every single day in June, and I was so sure the hottest day would be the longest one, the one with the most daylight. I even bragged to my cousin about it."

"What happened?" Salma asked.

"Nothing, that's the thing. The longest day came and went and it was just warm, not boiling. The really hot weeks didn't show up until weeks later, in the middle of July. I thought my thermometer was broken."

Cash laughed. "So what was it? Did you figure it out?"

Jasmine flipped open her own notebook, hunting for the page of numbers from last summer. "My grandma has a swimming pool, and I remembered something about it. Even on a scorching day, the shallow end barely warms up. The land and the water take time to heat through. So the hottest weather shows up weeks after the longest day, because everything is still warming up in between."

"So the longest day is like the starting gun," Salma said slowly, "and the heat arrives late."

"That's it exactly." Jasmine wrote it in big letters at the top of the page. She could already picture tomorrow: the class crowded around, Cash spinning the ball, Salma holding the flashlight while she explained the tilt and then, at the end, the surprise about the delayed heat. Not just the sun, she would say, but the ground and the oceans soaking it up like slow sponges.

"One more thing," Salma said, pointing at the broom handle sticking out of the ball. "What do you call that stick?"

"The axis. Basically the spine of the planet, the line it turns around." Jasmine reached over and nudged it a degree further sideways. "And here's the weird part. Nobody in my family can explain why I care this much about any of it. Curiosity like mine must not be hereditary."

Cash threw a piece of chalk at her. "Turn off the flashlight, save the batteries, and chalk the circle one more time."

Jasmine clicked the light off, and the backyard went dim and blue around them, the basketball still leaning on its broom handle in the grass.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
story:
At 7:42 on a Sunday night, Maeva flopped onto the couch with her phone and opened the group chat, where Serenity had already posted six messages in a row. The last one said: "Emmanuel is being INSANE about football stats again." Emmanuel replied with a screenshot of a headline that read QUARTERBACK POSTS PERFECT PASSER RATING, and then a single question: "why is perfect 158.3 and not 100?? who picked that??" Maeva sat up. She had been wondering the same thing since gym class on Friday, when Ms. Oliveira had put a game on the classroom projector during lunch and a kid near the window had shouted the number at the screen.

She typed: "maybe it's like a grade out of 100 but they added extra points for something." Serenity answered fast: "that makes no sense, you can't just add bonus to a scale." Maeva frowned at her phone. Serenity was annoyingly right about things like this. Emmanuel sent the actual formula, which was four lines long with division signs and subtraction in it, and Maeva actually laughed out loud, alone on the couch, which made her cat look at her with suspicion. "that's not a grade," she typed. "that's a machine." Emmanuel replied: "so it combines a bunch of passing stats into ONE number." Maeva read the line twice. Combinations. Like when Ms. Oliveira averaged the class's reading logs and one kid's 40 pages got squashed together with everyone else's 12.

Then she tested her idea. She typed: "ok so if it squishes a whole game into one number, two different games could come out the same number, right? like the same average from different stuff." Serenity, who was watching a recap with her dad, sent back: "my dad says the guy from Sunday threw only 14 passes and the guy from last month threw 31 and they BOTH got 158.3." Maeva inhaled so sharply she nearly snorted. It worked. The number was a doorway, not a photograph.

Emmanuel kept pushing: "but WHY 158.3." Maeva scrolled up and found the scale written under the formula: it ran from 0 at the bottom to a maximum of 158.3 at the top. "it's called passer rating," she typed, "and the top of the scale is 158.3, that's just the size of it." Then, because she wanted him to stop asking, she added: "a meter is 100 cm because somebody decided. same thing." Serenity sent a shark emoji and the words "size of it. like your ego."

Maeva put the phone face-down on her chest and stared at the ceiling, where a fly walked in a slow circle. On the screen, dimmed now, the last message glowed: Emmanuel typing. It buzzed three more times before she picked it up again. "so a perfect game and a perfect game aren't the same game," he wrote. Maeva smiled at the fly and typed back, "now you're getting it."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Specific details, like 'Grandma's red bicycle' instead of 'a bike', give an improv partner more to build on.
story:
Ryan stood in the drama camp's black-box studio, holding an invisible box that Mr. Goh had just handed him in mime. "This box has some stuff in it," Mr. Goh said. "Pass it along. Build a scene."

Antoine took the box from Ryan and opened it. "Nice stuff," he said, and handed it back. Khadija shrugged. "Cool stuff." The scene died in eight seconds, and everyone laughed the uncomfortable kind of laugh. Mr. Goh didn't. He just said, "Again," and walked to the back wall.

The camp was supposed to be prestigious, the kind with a waiting list, and on Friday one camper would be picked as the program's ambassador, sent to perform at the city theatre in front of real scouts. Khadija wanted it so badly she'd memorized the whole welcome packet, and Antoine wanted it too, though he pretended he didn't. Ryan mostly wanted to stop freezing every time a scene started.

They tried again, and again the box was just stuff. Ryan's mind went blank the way it had at the spring talent show, when he'd planned a monologue for weeks and then compressed the whole thing into thirty mumbled seconds because his partner had changed one line on him and he hadn't known what to do with it. That was the memory he kept returning to. He still wasn't sure whether he should have stuck to the script or let go of it.

Then, in the third round, Khadija grabbed the invisible box and said, "Careful, that's Grandma's red bicycle." Suddenly Antoine was adjusting a handlebar. Ryan found himself saying, "Yes, and the front wheel is still bent from when she raced the mailman down Hill Street." Khadija laughed and became the grandma, out of breath, demanding her bike back. The scene ran two whole minutes. It wasn't just luck, Ryan realized, watching the next pair go flat with vague offers. The specific thing, the named thing, was the difference. A bike gave you nothing to hold. Grandma's red bicycle gave you a person, a colour, a dent somewhere in its past.

He tested it the rest of the afternoon. "Yes, and it's a hamster," he'd say, and the scene would breathe. Vague offers, and it would stumble.

Afterward, Mr. Goh read names for the showcase, and the twist was not the one Ryan had braced for. Antoine got it, not Khadija, and not Ryan. Antoine stood frozen for a second, then looked straight at Khadija. "I can't do it alone," he said. "It was your bicycle that saved us today. Partner scene. Both of us, or I say no."

Khadija stared at him. "You'd give it up?"

"Split it and it's still more than I had in June," Antoine said.

Mr. Goh tapped his clipboard. "I'll allow it. But the ambassador picks the opening offer. Antoine?"

Antoine grinned and held out his hands, shaping an invisible box. "So. Grandma's red bicycle," he said.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed on 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah, making the trip west far faster than by wagon.
story:
Gabriel slid the photocopied settler's diary across the library table and glared at it, as if glaring might unlock it. Mr. Pierre had assigned each student a primary source and a question: why did people move west in the 1800s? Gabriel's diary belonged to a woman named Ruth who had crossed Nebraska in a wagon in 1865, and so far all she talked about was dust, oxen, and a broken wheel.

"Find anything?" asked Giuseppe, who had a stack of newspaper clippings and a smug look.

"Oxen," Gabriel said. "My whole primary source is oxen." The embarrassment from yesterday's class still stung, when he had guessed that people moved west because they were "bored," and Cian had laughed so hard he knocked over his chair. Gabriel turned another page, and there it was, in cramped brown ink: Ruth's brother had written to her from Sacramento, and she had copied his letter into the diary word for word.

Dear Ruth, the letter began. We came out on the cars, not the trail. What took you six months of wagon and walking took us days on the new train. It runs clear across to California now. Come while the fare is cheap.

Gabriel read it three times. Six months against days. He checked the diary's front page again. Ruth crossed in 1865, and she was still on the trail when her brother wrote. He pulled over the class timeline and ran his finger down it. There. The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was finished on 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah. He sat back. So Ruth's brother could not have ridden a finished railroad in 1865, because it did not exist yet. The letter had to be later, after Ruth had settled, urging her to come back or bring the rest of the family. That meant the railroad changed everything: the same trip, from months in a wagon to days in a train.

He tested the idea out loud, quietly, then wrote it in the margin: after 1869, the trip west became far faster, so more people could go. It sounded almost coherent to him, like a real historian's argument. Mr. Pierre drifted past, read the margin, and nodded once, which Mr. Pierre almost never did.

At the next class, Gabriel stood up and told the whole thing: the diary, the letter, the date, the difference it made. Cian raised his hand. "So the settlers who went by wagon," he said, "they went before the easy way existed?" Gabriel nodded, thinking of Ruth pushing a wagon through dust, only to have the world change behind her.

"Would you have gone?" Cian asked.

Gabriel looked down at the diary's last page, where Ruth had written, We are here. "I don't know yet," he said, and started reading again.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: True lilies are highly toxic to cats, so they are unsafe to keep in a home with a cat.
story:
The kitten rode home in a cardboard box with holes punched in the top, and Paisley kept one finger through a hole the whole way so Mochi could sniff it. She had read the care sheet twice on the bus. Water, food, a litter box, a warm corner. What the sheet had not mentioned was the bouquet waiting on the kitchen table: tall white flowers with orange centers, tied with a ribbon, a birthday card stuck in among the stems. "From your aunt," her mom said. "Aren't they gorgeous?"

Paisley thought they were, but something nagged at her, a slow intuition that she couldn't quite put into words. Mochi had already wriggled out of the box and was sniffing along the table leg, tail up, interested. Paisley picked the kitten up and carried her to the other side of the room. Then she fetched her library book about cats, the one with the plant chapter, and flipped until she found a page marked with a warning sign. There they were, the same trumpet-shaped flowers. True lilies are highly toxic to cats, the book said, so they are unsafe to keep in a home with a cat. Even the flowers alone could hurt one.

"So they can't just sit on a high shelf?" her mom asked, watching Paisley carry the vase toward the door.

"Kittens climb," Paisley said. "And fallen leaves would obstruct nothing, they'd just be petals on the floor where she walks. It's not one big danger, it's lots of small chances, and they're cumulative." She set the vase on the porch steps, well outside, then went back and checked under the table for any dropped leaves or pollen dust. She found two orange smears of pollen on the wood and wiped them up with a paper towel, twice, and then once more for good measure.

The next day Justin came over to meet Mochi, and he brought his little notebook of questions, because he was that kind of kid. "How did you know about the flowers?" he asked, crouching where Mochi was batting a bottle cap across the floor.

"I didn't, at first," Paisley said. "I only knew that my brain felt funny about them. So I tested it. I looked it up, and then I checked every room for petals, like the danger was something I could hunt down." She pointed at the porch, where the lilies stood in the sun, beautiful and far away. "Best birthday flowers ever, though. They just live outside now."

Mochi pounced on the bottle cap and skidded under the chair, ears back, thrilled.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Near the ends of long bones are growth plates made of cartilage, where bones lengthen during childhood; a break through a growth plate can affect how the bone grows.
story:
The waiting room had a poster of migratory geese above the chairs, and Caleb stared at it so he wouldn't look at his arm, which was bent in a way arms should not bend. His friend Tatum sat beside him, holding Caleb's shoe, which had come off when they'd pried his fingers out of the climbing gym's yellow wall.

"You were on the easy route," Tatum said. "The easy route. My grandmother could do the easy route."

"Your grandmother does water aerobics. She'd crush it." Caleb's voice came out thin. He was starting to perspire under the paper blanket, even though the room was cold. "Tatum, hold my hand? Not the broken one."

"The broken one is the only one you need held, but fine." Tatum took the good hand and squeezed.

A doctor in blue scrubs came out and looked at the X-rays taped to a light box. "Good news," she said. "The break missed your growth plate."

"Wait." Caleb leaned forward. "Why is that good news? What's a growth plate?"

"Near the ends of long bones, there's a growth plate made of cartilage. That's where your bones lengthen while you're a kid. A break through it can affect how the bone grows. Yours missed it by a mile."

Caleb studied the X-ray. So his arm was like the geese on the poster, he thought. It had a route it was supposed to travel, a hidden map. He'd seen a film in science class about bird adaptations, how wings were shaped for the journey. His arm had its own map, drawn in cartilage, and he'd almost torn through it without ever knowing it was there.

"So if the crack had gone two centimeters down," he said slowly, pointing, "this arm might have stopped growing? And the other one wouldn't?"

"That's right," the doctor said. "You'd have one short arm. We'd have to keep an eye on it for years."

Tatum looked a little pale. "Okay, that's the last time I say anything about your climbing."

An hour later, Caleb's arm was wrapped in bright orange plaster, and Tatum was asking the nurse to sign it. Mr. De Vries arrived from the climbing gym, still in his harness, and set down a bag of chips and a Get Well balloon shaped like a flamingo.

"I called your mom," Mr. De Vries said. "She's on her way. And Caleb, your belay technique was actually excellent. Your foot placement was the problem, and feet are fixable."

"Everything's fixable," Caleb said, examining the cast. "The map's still intact."

Tatum wrote on the orange plaster in thick marker: NEXT TIME, TAKE THE STAIRS.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: You may never divide both sides of an equation by zero, because division by zero has no answer.
story:
Brody had come to math club for the cookies, and he was not ashamed of that. He had stayed for the equations, which was more embarrassing. Ms. Moretti had shown them how to solve things like 3x plus 5 equals 14 by doing the same thing to both sides, and Brody had discovered he liked it. It felt like a fair trade. Whatever you did to one side, you had to do to the other, no exceptions, no sneaking.

Then Baby stood up at the whiteboard and announced that he could prove 1 equals 2.

"You can't," said Lane, who was nominating herself for the job of saying "you can't" to everything today.

"Watch," said Baby. He wrote fast. Let a equal b, he began. Then a times a equals a times b, so a squared equals ab. He subtracted b squared from both sides, factored one side, divided both sides by (a minus b), and landed on a equals b. Then, since he'd started by saying a equals b, he plugged in 1 for a and 2 for b, and there it was: 1 equals 2. He put the marker down like a magician releasing a dove.

Lane said "you can't" three more times but could not say where the trick was. Ms. Moretti sat on the edge of the desk with her arms crossed and, worse, a small smile, which meant she knew and was not going to help. Brody copied the proof into his notebook and went line by line, because a proof was like a machine, and machines had one part that broke.

He found it at the division. Baby had divided both sides by (a minus b). But the very first line said a equals b. So a minus b was zero. Brody raised his hand so fast his chair tipped.

"You divided by zero," he said. "And a equals b, so a minus b is zero, and you divided by that."

Baby looked at his own board. The smile slid off his face slowly, the way ice melts when nobody wants it to.

"You may never divide both sides by zero," Brody went on, standing now, pointing at the line with his pencil. "Division by zero has no answer. It's not infinity, it's not one, it's nothing. That step just isn't allowed."

"Then my proof is a descendant of one illegal move," Baby said sadly. "All that work for nothing."

"Voluntary confession looks good on you, though," said Lane.

Ms. Moretti held out the plate of cookies toward Brody. He took two, one for each side.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Research on expert performers has found that how someone practices, focusing on specific weak spots, matters more than simply playing a piece many times.
story:
The guitar had belonged to Emily's grandfather, and it lived in the spare room between a stack of old newspapers and a shelf of flammable wood polish, which her grandmother mentioned every single time Emily carried the case past the shelf. Emily had been practicing the same song for eleven days, playing it from start to finish, start to finish, start to finish. On Saturday she played it for Marcus over a video call, and she crashed at exactly the same place she always crashed.

"Four measures," Marcus said, leaning toward his screen. "You got through everything else fine. Even the fast part."

Emily set the guitar flat on her lap and looked at the four measures on the page. She had played this song at least sixty times. If playing it more times were the answer, she should have fixed the mistake by now. The mistake stayed anyway, like a loose stair that never fixed itself no matter how many times you walked up the stairs. "It's not that I need to play the whole song more," she said slowly. "It's that I need to play this part differently. Maybe just this part, over and over, until my hands can coordinate on their own." Her left hand and her right hand disagreed at that spot, one jumping early while the other held on too long, and no amount of playing the easy parts was going to teach them anything new.

So she tried it. She played only the four measures, ten times, twenty times, slowly first and then faster. Her grandmother brought in lemonade and stayed to listen, and when Emily flinched at the same stumble, her grandmother said, "That bit again," and Emily nodded and did it again. Halfway through the afternoon she stopped missing it. Then she started the four measures from the measure before, so her fingers would learn how to arrive at the hard part instead of only how to survive it. When she finally played the whole song through, the trouble spot came and went like a door that had been oiled.

On Sunday she called Marcus again and played the entire piece without stopping. He held up both hands. "Yesterday you couldn't get through that part once."

"I didn't practice the song today," Emily said. "I practiced the four measures." She told him she thought that was the whole secret, that working on the weak spots mattered more than running through the piece a bunch of times, and that she was going to test it on the second song in the book, which had two bad spots instead of one. "One at a time," she said. "Worst spot first."

Her grandmother appeared in the doorway with a duster. "Your grandfather did the same thing, you know. He'd sit in that chair for an hour with one phrase, driving the neighbours half mad." She pointed the duster at the shelf. "And when you put that guitar back, keep it away from the polish. It's flammable, that stuff." Emily laughed, laid the guitar in its case, and clicked the latches shut one at a time, like two small hands finally agreeing on something.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Psychologists often separate fear, a reaction to a threat happening now, from anxiety, worry about a threat that might happen in the future.
story:
Daniel found his brother's old psychology textbook open on the kitchen table, but that wasn't why he'd come downstairs. He'd come down because his stomach hurt again, the fourth morning in a row, and he was tired of pretending it was the cereal.

"You look like a ghost," said Dastan, who had knocked on the door twenty minutes ago and let himself in the way he always did. "Is it the tryout?"

"It's Friday," Daniel said. "It's Tuesday."

"So?" Dastan dropped onto a chair and spun the textbook toward himself. "Roger told me you didn't sleep at his sleepover. You kept getting up to drink water."

Daniel sat down across from him. He hadn't told anyone about the sleepover, not even Roger. Last Saturday, in the dark of Roger's living room, he had lain on the floor imagining the whole tryout: the gym, the whistle, the coach's clipboard, and then the moment he fumbled the ball in front of everyone. The humiliation he pictured had felt so real that his heart had pounded as though he were standing on the court right then. Except he wasn't. He was on a sleeping bag between two friends, perfectly safe.

He flipped the textbook pages without reading them at first. Then a line caught his eye. Fear, it said, is a reaction to a threat happening now. Anxiety is worry about a threat that might happen in the future.

"That's it," Daniel said quietly.

"That's what?"

"Read it. I'm not scared of the kitchen table. There's no threat here. It's all Friday stuff, stuff that hasn't even happened yet." He tapped the page. "So it's anxiety, not fear."

Dastan squinted. "So?"

"So fear is when the dog is actually chasing you. Anxiety is when you spend four days worrying about a dog that might never chase you." Daniel stood up. "I keep reacting like the tryout is happening now. It isn't. It's a maybe."
