He went to the counter, found a pencil, and drafted a sign on the back of a grocery receipt. NOT FRIDAY YET, it said. He taped it to the refrigerator, right at eye level, where he'd see it every time he came for water in the night.

"Boundaries," Dastan said, reading over his shoulder. "Like you're telling your brain where it's allowed to go."

"Something like that."

The stomach ache didn't vanish, but by Thursday Daniel noticed it came and went, a temporary visitor instead of a permanent roommate, and each time it arrived he looked at the sign and it loosened its grip a little.

Friday came at last. Daniel walked into the gym with his sneakers squeaking on the floor. The whistle blew. The coach tossed him the ball.

"Pick it up, kid," the coach called. "It's just a warm-up."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The rule of thirds is a composition guideline that divides a picture into a three-by-three grid and places the main subject along those lines or where they cross.
story:
Keira pressed her pencil so hard against the sketchpad that the tip snapped. Her lopsided drawing of the camp lake sat dead in the middle of the page, and it looked like every postcard in the camp gift shop, only worse. The art show was tomorrow night, and she had promised Claudia and Zarah something good.

"It's boring," Claudia said, leaning over her shoulder on the porch of the craft cabin. "Sorry. But it's boring."

"I know it's boring." Keira flipped to a fresh page. "The lake's not boring. My drawing is."

Zarah held up her own painting, a canoe tucked into the bottom corner of her canvas. "Mr. Mansour said mine was strong. I don't even know what I did."

Keira looked at Zarah's painting, then at Claudia's collage, where a heron stood off to the left of a big sky. Both of them had put their subjects away from the center. All morning she had noticed the same thing on the cabin's corkboard, where the best pieces from past summers hung: an owl beside a moon, a pine tree hugging one side. Nothing sat in the exact middle except her lake.

"Wait," she said slowly. "Can I borrow your pencil for a second?" She took Claudia's pencil and laid it flat across Zarah's canvas, one third of the way up from the bottom. The canoe's hull rested right along it. She turned the pencil sideways and laid it one third in from the left edge, and it crossed the heron in Claudia's collage almost exactly. Her heart sped up. "Try mine."

She drew two lines across her blank page, dividing it into a three-by-three grid, then two more lines the other way. Where the lines crossed near the top left, she sketched a tiny sailboat. She placed the far shore along the lower line instead of floating it in the middle of the paper. Was that really all it took? She shaded the sky, stepped back, and squinted. The lake suddenly seemed to go on forever.

"Whoa," Claudia said.

At the critique session that evening, Mr. Mansour held Keira's drawing up to the porch light. "Interesting," he said. "Where did you learn the rule of thirds?"

"Is that what it's called?" Keira grinned. "I made Zarah's painting tell me."

"You were reckless with that pencil grid," he said, "and it worked." He pinned the drawing to the corkboard, a little off center, where the best pieces thrived.

Keira went to find Zarah. "Your canoe taught me everything," she said. "Tomorrow I'm teaching you."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Tropical rainforests lie near the equator, where strong sunlight heats moist air that rises, cools and forms clouds, often bringing heavy afternoon rain.
story:
Zack lagged behind the others on the switchback trail, holding his worksheet against a rock so the wind wouldn't take it. Two graphs stared up at him: one for the Sonoran Desert, where rainfall barely registered month after month, and one for a rainforest in the Amazon, where the bars jumped high and jagged. He was supposed to compare them, but the numbers refused to say anything to him. Ms. Weiss had said the answers were hiding in plain sight, which felt like a joke, because nothing about the assignment looked plain at all.

"Still stuck on the climate thing?" Giuliano called back. Giuliano wanted to finish first, as always, so he could pull out his phone and show everyone the photos from his uncle's trip to the Amazon. He'd been talking about them since the bus.

"Rainforests get a ton of rain, deserts don't. There. Done," Zack muttered, shoving the paper in his pocket. But he knew that answer was worth about two points out of ten. He remembered last week, sitting in the stuffy classroom with the AC rattling, staring at the same graphs while Jamie drew little clouds in the margins and got a better grade. That still stung.

At the overlook, Giuliano got his wish. He held up his phone, and everyone leaned in. "Look at these. My uncle took them on the same day." The first photo showed a river winding under a wide blue sky, tall trees steaming in the light. The second, stamped four hours later, showed the same trees bent under a black wall of storm, rain hammering the water. "Morning was clear," Giuliano said. "Every morning was clear. Then boom, every afternoon."

Zack pulled his worksheet back out. His water bottle sat beside it, and the sun cut through it, throwing a small wobbling prism of colors across the paper, right over the rainforest graph. He stared. Clear mornings, storms every afternoon, near the equator. Strong sunlight heats the moist air, the air rises, cools, forms clouds, and the rain comes. That was why the bars fluctuated so wildly, week to week but always heavy, always returning. The desert graph never did that; it just sat there flat. "I've got it," he said. "Near the equator the sunlight's strong, and it heats the moist air. The air rises, cools, forms clouds, and you get those afternoon storms. That's why his uncle's photos go blue sky, then downpour, every single day."

Ms. Weiss, a few steps behind, raised an eyebrow at him. "So is that pattern probable anywhere else, or is it tied to the equator?"

Zack tapped the desert graph, where the rainfall line lay flat as the trail below them. "Tied to the equator. This place never gets that moist air rising." He grabbed his pencil and started writing, fast, before the thought could escape.

"So can I see your paper when you're done?" Giuliano asked, peering over his shoulder. "Because my uncle has more photos, and I want to know what's in them."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The Panic of 1837 caused a long economic depression in the United States, and many ruined farmers later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land.
story:
The diary sat behind glass under a dim light, open to a page written in cramped brown ink. Vincent leaned closer until his breath fogged the case. His worksheet had one question on it, the one Ms. López had repeated twice on the bus: "Use this diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s." He had hoped for an answer in the first paragraph, something obvious like gold or adventure.

"We lost the farm in June," the settler had written. "The bank took it, and there is nothing left here for us. We will go where the land is cheap and the soil is black." Vincent read it three times. He had been ready to write that the family wanted wide open spaces, because that was what the mural in the hallway showed, wagons rolling through golden grass. Now he wasn't sure that was true at all.

Reese appeared beside him with her phone out, photographing a broken plow. "Find anything?" she asked.

"I think I had it backwards," Vincent said. "They didn't leave because they wanted to. They left because they had to. Something went wrong back east. But the diary doesn't say what, and I can't write 'something went wrong' on the sheet."

Jakub waved them over from a display case near the window, where an information panel caught the afternoon light. The glass over one paragraph was opaque with age, but the heading above it was clear: The Panic of 1837. "Hey, is this the year in your diary?" Jakub asked.

Vincent checked the faded date at the top of the page. It matched. Below the heading, the panel explained that the Panic of 1837 caused a long economic depression in the United States. That was the hidden hinge, he realized, the thing the whole diary turned on. The banks failed, farms were ruined, and many of those ruined farmers later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land. He copied the words down carefully, then read them again to make sure he had them right.

Ms. López came past with her hands in her cardigan pockets. "How's it going?" she asked.

Vincent held up his notes. "The family didn't move for adventure. They lost their farm in the Panic of 1837, and it caused a depression, so they went west for cheap land. The diary says the soil was black. That's why they risked the trail."

"That's using a primary source," Ms. López said, and moved on toward the maps at the far wall.

On the bus home, Vincent wrote his paragraph, quoting the diary line about the bank and the cheap land beside it. He had almost finished when he turned back to his photo of the case and noticed something he had missed. In the margin of the diary page, in smaller ink, the settler had added a note: "We cherish the memory of our old home, but we do not regret leaving." Vincent read it twice, then added one more sentence to his paragraph and closed his notebook as the museum gates slid out of view.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: On the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967, both changing residence and changing schools are listed as life events that require readjustment.
story:
Lauren sat on her bedroom floor with a roll of packing tape in her lap, because in two weeks the moving truck would come and take everything to Millbrook, four hours away. Her best friend Emerson was sprawled across the bed, popping bubble wrap one bubble at a time, which was supposed to be helpful but mostly wasn't.

"I keep thinking something's wrong with me," Lauren admitted. "I'm tired all the time and I got a headache at school Tuesday, and I haven't even moved yet. I'm not even sick."

Emerson stopped popping. "Maybe you're sick of boxes."

That actually made sense. Lauren had been counting them: eleven in the garage, six in the hall, four in her room, and the number kept climbing. She grabbed her notebook and wrote "boxes" at the top of a page. Underneath she made two columns, one for the new house and one for the new school, and wrote down everything different. New street. New room. New teacher. New desk. New bus route. The two lists were almost the same length, which felt like a clue.

The next morning she found the school counselor's pamphlet stuck inside a library book about the brain, a book she'd borrowed because a poster in science class had the word neuron on it and she'd wondered what one was. The pamphlet was for new students, with a quiz inside. "Feeling tired, run-down, or achy after a move is common," it said. "On the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967, both changing residence and changing schools are listed as life events that require readjustment." She read the sentence three times. Her two lists weren't just sad feelings; they were both on an actual scale, counted like pounds on a scale at the doctor's office. Nothing was broken. Her body was just doing a lot of lifting.

She tested it. That afternoon she taped two boxes instead of six, then rode her bike to the end of the street and back, and by dinner her headache had faded to almost nothing. Her mom noticed her actually eating her spaghetti and raised an eyebrow. "Better," Lauren said, and didn't explain, because the whole idea still felt fragile, like the frail little bookmark that had come out of the library book.

That night she wrote to Emerson on notebook paper, since Emerson had refused to say goodbye in person until the actual last day.

Dear Emerson. I figured out why I've been weird. There's a thing called the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967, and moving house and changing schools are both on it, listed as life events that require readjustment. BOTH, at the same time, for me. So it's not that I'm falling apart. It's that two big things coincide this month, and I get to be tired without it meaning anything is wrong. I'm still going to miss you terrible amounts. But my new plan is to unpack one box a day, find the library first, and write to you every Sunday. Love, Lauren.

She folded the letter, stamped it, and set it on the kitchen counter next to her mom's keys where it couldn't be missed. Then she went upstairs and wrote "1" at the top of a fresh page.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1, showing no significant home advantage.
story:
Logan stood at the boards with Milania and Maximus, watching the championship game between two teams from across town. His dad had driven them all to the rink, and the home team was down by one goal with six minutes left in the third period. The stands behind them were packed, and everyone was screaming every time the home team touched the puck.

"Listen to that," Maximus shouted over the noise. "This is why we're going to win. Home crowd, home ice. It has to help."

Logan wasn't so sure. He had been thinking about it since the second period, when the home team took two penalties in a row and the crowd's cheering didn't seem to change anything. He remembered something his uncle had told him in the fall, something that had stuck because the numbers were so strange. During the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1. That was no significant home advantage at all, basically a coin flip.

"Wait," Logan said. "In the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1. No home advantage. Not even a little."

"That's football," Milania said. "Hockey's different."

"Maybe," Logan said. "But if a whole season of NFL games shows the crowd doesn't matter, why would it matter here?" He wanted to test it. He told them his plan: for the next three minutes, nobody cheers. They would just watch what the home team did in the quiet, and compare it to the loud stretches.

Maximus groaned but agreed, because there were only five minutes left and the experiment had to happen now or never. The three of them went silent. Logan tracked the plays, keeping a count in his head the way he kept stats for his own team. In the quiet stretch, the home team forced a turnover, got a shot on net, and drew a penalty. The power play started with two minutes forty left on the clock.

"See," Milania whispered, though she didn't dare cheer yet.

The home team moved the puck around the zone in a calm, stable pattern, patient and unhurried, as if the noise had nothing to do with anything. Logan tried to extract a cleaner conclusion from his little experiment, but three quiet minutes against a season of NFL data wasn't much logic to build on. Still, nobody was about to argue with 127-128-1.

The winger one-timed a pass from the corner and the goalie got a piece of it but not enough. Tie game. The whole rink erupted, and Maximus turned to Logan with his hands up.

"Okay, so was that the crowd or was that us being quiet?" he yelled.

"Try to figure it out," Logan said, and he cupped his hands around his mouth and cheered louder than anyone.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: In his book Opticks, first published in 1704, Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early form of the color wheel.
story:
Isabelle spread her paint chips across the kitchen table like a hand of cards. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, and then, stubbornly, nothing. The assignment was a color wheel for Mr. Lau's art class, due Friday, and hers had a gap where violet met red again. She couldn't make the circle close.

"It's not going to close," she said to Steven, who sat across from her eating crackers and offering no help whatsoever. "A wheel goes all the way around. Mine just stops."

"Maybe wheels aren't supposed to close," Steven said. "Like a rainbow. Rainbows don't wrap around."

"Rainbows aren't wheels." She tapped the table. "Somebody drew the first one of these, right? Somebody had to figure out the order." She grabbed her phone and typed: who made the first color wheel.

Steven leaned over, crumbs falling on her paint chips. "What does it say?"

"It says Isaac Newton." She read faster, smiling. "In his book Opticks, first published in 1704, he arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle." She read it aloud twice so it would stick. "So the first person to bend the rainbow into a loop was Newton."

"Wait, gravity Newton? Apple-on-the-head Newton?"

"The same one." She couldn't stop grinning. "So if Newton could close the circle, the circle can close. I'm just doing something wrong." She lined up her chips again and squinted down the row. "There has to be something between violet and red. A color that goes both ways, sort of."

"Like what, purple-red?" Steven stacked a cracker on his cracker. "That's not a color."

But she was already mixing, dragging a brush through red and adding violet a little at a time. The first attempt looked like a bruise. The second looked like an infection, blotchy and sour. "Gross," she said, delighted anyway, because gross meant she was still experimenting.

"Wash the brush," Steven said. "Your red is contaminating everything. That's why your mixes keep coming out muddy."

She stopped. That was the hidden problem, wasn't it, the thing she couldn't see directly: her brush carried leftover red into every mixture, turning her colors brown before she even began. She rinsed the brush until the water ran clean, then started fresh with a sparse dab of red, just the smallest touch, and blended violet in slowly. This time the color came out glowing, like the last sliver of light before the sky goes dark.

"Write the name on the back," Steven said, pointing at her sketchbook. "You'll forget by Friday."

She flipped it over and printed: Newton, Opticks, 1704, colors of the spectrum in a circle. Then she cut a perfect chip from her new paint, set it into the gap between violet and red, and the wheel closed at last, a full ring of color with no beginning and no end.

"Take a picture before anything dries weird," Steven said, holding out her phone.

Isabelle framed the wheel on the table, the kitchen light catching every hue in order, and pressed the button.

fact: Muscles in a limb kept still in a cast weaken and shrink, which is why an arm often looks thinner when the cast comes off.
story:
"You've got ten minutes before they call you back," Ewan said, tapping the cast with his pen. "Everybody in shop class signed except Ace, and he's on his way. If you get it off before he shows up, that's it. Permanent. No second chances."

Lincoln looked at his arm, white and graffiti-covered, riding shotgun in the waiting room chair. He had spent six weeks defending that cast from table edges and doorframes, and now that the appointment to remove it had finally arrived, he felt oddly unwilling to let it go. "He'll make it," Lincoln said. "Ace runs everywhere."

Six weeks ago he had made a different choice, and he kept turning it over while the receptionist clicked her keyboard. The ramp behind the school, the skateboard he knew was cracked along the hull, the moment he could have bailed and didn't. He had told himself the board would hold. It hadn't. Now Ace was sprinting across town so he wouldn't lose his chance to write on the evidence.

"Lincoln?" A nurse held the door open, and the saw on the counter behind her made a sound like a dying vacuum.

"Wait," Lincoln said. "One more signature. Two minutes."

She checked her watch and let them hover in the doorway. Ewan wrote his name in block letters and then, underneath, drew a dinosaur. "An extinct tyrannosaurus," he announced. "Tiny arms. Like yours are gonna be." He laughed at his own joke.

"That doesn't even make sense," Lincoln said, but a worry started in him anyway. He flexed his fingers inside the cast, the way the nurse had told him to do every day, and tried to remember whether he actually had. Some days, sure. But most days he'd just let the arm hang there in its shell, doing nothing, while he used the other one for everything. Opening lockers. Carrying his tray. Writing. If a bone needed rest to heal, maybe the rest of the arm needed work to stay an arm. He couldn't see inside the plaster to check. He could only test it.

So while they waited, he gripped the armrest and squeezed, hard, over and over, feeling something small tighten deep under the cast. Ewan raised an eyebrow. "Getting in one last workout before retirement?"

"Something like that," Lincoln said.

Ace skidded through the door with the pen already uncapped, signed upside down on Lincoln's wrist, and patted the cast like a good horse. Then the nurse pointed at the chair, and the saw buzzed, and the plaster split open like a seedpod.

The arm that emerged was pale and strange. Lincoln held both arms out side by side, and his stomach dropped. The right one was noticeably thinner than the left, the left suddenly magnified by comparison, bulky and brown next to a white, shrunken stick. He squeezed his right hand around the pen Ace had left behind. The grip felt weak, like the arm belonged to somebody younger.

"Is that normal?" he asked the nurse, keeping his voice steady.

"Happens every time," she said. "Muscles kept still in a cast weaken and shrink. It'll build back with use."

Mr. Levy, the doctor, came in and rotated the wrist, pressing here and there, and pronounced the bone healed. "Want to take the pen home?" he asked. "You'll need something to squeeze."

Lincoln closed his fist around it and looked at his two arms lying in his lap, mismatched. Ace leaned over and said, "So the skateboard thing. You'd do it again, or not?"

Lincoln looked at the arm for a long moment. "Ask me in six weeks," he said, and pocketed the pen.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Near the equator, sunlight stays fairly direct all year, so temperatures change little and many places have wet and dry seasons instead of warm and cold ones.
story:
Mr. Demir put a globe, a flashlight, and an orange on the table at the front of the room, and Aaron's hand shot up before the question was even finished. "You have to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons," Mr. Demir said. "Presentations on Friday. You can use anything on this table, but I'm being frugal with my batteries, so practice your setup first." Aaron was already planning: flashlight as the sun, globe as Earth, tilt it, and the answer would just appear.

There was one problem. Wallace had moved here in September from a city near the equator, and when Aaron mentioned the presentation at lunch, Wallace laughed so hard he knocked over his milk. "Four seasons?" Wallace said. "Warm season, cold season? Where I'm from, we have a wet season and a dry season. That's it. Nobody talks about winter." Bruno shrugged like this was no big deal, but Aaron couldn't stop thinking about it. If the tilt caused seasons, why didn't Wallace's home have them?

That night Aaron borrowed his mother's flashlight and a soccer ball, and he drew a crooked line through the ball with chalk for the axis. In his dark bedroom he held the flashlight steady and spun the ball around it, tilted. He leaned closer, watching the bright spot of light crawl across the chalk. At the top of the ball the spot landed small and fierce. At the middle, near where he imagined Wallace's city, the spot stayed round and steady, and here was the strange part: as he walked the ball around the flashlight, that middle spot barely changed. It was fairly direct the whole year round.

He grabbed his notebook. "So the light near the middle doesn't turn slanted like it does up here," he muttered. If the light stays direct, then the temperature wouldn't swing, so no warm and cold seasons. He wrote it out twice to be sure it made sense, then texted Wallace: ask your mom if the temperature changes much through the year. The reply came back in a minute: she says barely at all, just rain or no rain.

On Friday, Aaron set up the flashlight and the globe in front of the class, tilted the globe, and walked it in a slow circle. "Watch the beam up here," he said, pointing near the top. "It spreads out and weakens for half the trip, then tightens up for the other half. That's our year." Then he tapped Wallace's desk. "Tell them where you're from." Wallace stood up, grinning. "Near the equator. The sunlight stays fairly direct all year, so it barely changes temperature. We get wet and dry seasons instead." Aaron spun the globe one more time so the class could see the steady bright spot riding the middle, and Mr. Demir clicked off the flashlight and said, "Now that is a presentation."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Repeating an experiment several times and averaging the results reduces the effect of random errors in any single trial.
story:
The meeting room at the public library smelled like pencil shavings and old carpet, and Elena had claimed the far table with her model catapult, three meter sticks, and a bag of marshmallows she was supposed to be launching, not eating. Axton sat across from her, drafting the poster on graph paper, while Louis guarded the door in case the eccentric librarian with the cat-shaped glasses came back to remind them, again, that this was a quiet zone.

"Launch one," Elena announced, pulled the arm back, and let go. The marshmallow sailed over the meter sticks, bounced off the window, and rolled under the microfiche cabinet. All three of them froze. "That was like four meters," Louis whispered, retrieving it with a ruler because neither of them wanted to touch the dust down there. Elena wrote 4.0 in her notebook and frowned at it. The second launch barely cleared one meter. She looked from the notebook to the catapult and back, as if one of them were lying.

"Maybe it hates you," Axton offered. "Maybe it's the rubber band. It's this stretchy polymer stuff, and it never pulls the same way twice." Elena turned that over in her head. If the band pulled differently every time, then no single launch told her anything real about the catapult. What she needed was the number underneath all the wobbly ones. "We're doing ten," she said, "and then we average." She felt a little bad about the noise, so when the librarian peeked in, Elena showed her the notebook and promised they'd postpone the loud part until the room was empty. The librarian said marshmallows were the quietest ammunition she'd ever seen in that room, and left them a broom.

They ran the trials while Axton called out distances and Louis marked landing spots with sticky notes. Two meters, then almost three, then a pathetic half meter that Louis insisted they name Gerald. Elena added all ten numbers, divided, and got 2.3 meters. She circled it twice. One launch had said four. One had said half a meter. The average sat right in the middle, steady, like something true.

"It's still the same catapult," Axton said, tapping her notebook. "You just made it tell the truth."

Elena grinned and loaded one last marshmallow, the ceremonial Gerald Two. "For science," she said, and let it fly.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Hanukkah menorah, or hanukkiah, has nine branches: eight for the eight nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others.
story:
On the third night of Hanukkah, Easton was setting the hanukkiah on the windowsill when his friend Teo arrived, still holding the note Easton's mom had written inviting him over: "Come at sundown, bring an appetite." Teo stared at the menorah with his coat half off. "Wait," he said. "Hanukkah is eight nights, right? Why does that thing have nine spots for candles?"

Easton opened his mouth and then closed it, because he realized he had never actually counted. He had lit the candles every night of his life, but always in the dark, always in a hurry, always with his little sister leaning on his elbow. "Hold on," he said, and he carried the hanukkiah to the kitchen table under the bright light. He touched each empty holder with his finger, one at a time, like a diligent student taking attendance. Four on one side, four on the other, and one standing apart in the middle, raised a little higher than the rest. "There are nine," he admitted. "But Hanukkah is eight nights. I know that part for sure."

He thought about the middle one, the tall one, and about what he did with it every night. It was a reflex by now, reaching for that candle first, lighting it with the match, and only then touching its flame to the others. He never lit the side candles from the match itself. He tested the idea out loud, walking his fingers through the motions in the air. "We always light the middle one first, and it lights all the rest. It's not one of the eight, it's a helper." His dad, passing through with a plate of latkes, heard the last word and nodded. "The shamash," he said, and kept walking.

"So the middle candle is like the teacher's assistant," Teo said slowly, "and the eight around it are the actual nights." Easton grinned and set the hanukkiah back on the windowsill. They placed three candles for the third night, plus the shamash in the middle, and Easton's mom turned off the overhead light. In the dark, Easton lit the shamash first, watched Teo's face glow orange, and used the helper flame to light the three candles from left to right while his dad sang the blessing and his sister tried to petition her way into getting an extra sufganiyeh before dinner.

Later, Teo wrote Easton a text before he even got home: "Tell your mom thanks. Also I'm counting candles at my grandma's church now, just to check." Easton laughed and typed back, "Count the ones in the middle."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: In the United States, a large CDC survey found the median age of a girl's first period is about 12 years old, with a wide normal range around it.
story:
Kate had been carrying the question around for two weeks like a stone in her pocket, and tonight, at Cecilia's kitchen table with popcorn between them, she finally set it down. "Can I ask you something weird?" she said.

Cecilia raised an eyebrow and pushed the bowl closer, which Kate took as a yes. "My sister got her first period when she was almost fourteen," Kate said, keeping her voice low even though they were alone. "And I keep thinking, okay, so that's the pattern, that's when it happens. But I don't actually know if that's a pattern or just... her."

"My sister was eleven," Cecilia said. "Eleven and a half. She told my mom in the middle of Thanksgiving dinner." She laughed, then stopped laughing when she saw Kate's face. "Wait, are you worried?"

"A little." Kate picked up a kernel and put it back down. "Because if my sister was almost fourteen and I'm thirteen and it hasn't happened yet, maybe something's wrong with me. Or maybe it's just different for everybody. I can't tell, because you can't see it coming. There's no preview."

Cecilia drummed her fingers on the table. "We could ask my sister. She reads everything. She wants to work for some big health corporation someday, so she memorizes studies like they're song lyrics." She stood up so fast the popcorn bowl rattled, and Kate followed her down the hall to her sister's room, feeling like she was walking toward an ominous black door in a video game even though it was just beige with a band poster on it.

Cecilia's sister was lying on her bed with headphones in, but she pulled one out when they hovered in the doorway. She listened to the whole stammered question without smirking, which Kate appreciated more than she could say. "There was a big CDC survey about this," the sister said. "The median age for a girl's first period in the United States is about twelve. But the normal range around it is really wide."

"Median," Kate repeated. "So half before twelve, half after?"

"Basically. So fourteen isn't strange, and eleven isn't strange either. It's a range, not a deadline." She put her headphone back in, then took it out again. "And you don't need to incorporate anything new into your life yet. Just keep a couple of supplies in your backpack and get on with things."

Back in the kitchen, Cecilia dumped the stale popcorn into the trash and refilled the bowl from a fresh bag she'd been saving, and they watched a movie with the volume low. Kate kept thinking about the word median, turning it over, deciding it was a good word, sturdier than average.

"Hey," Cecilia said during a commercial. "If it happens when you're here, I've got supplies in the bathroom cabinet, second shelf. My sister restocks it like she's running a corporation."

"Deal," Kate said, and tossed a piece of popcorn at her.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when proteins in wheat flour mix with water, and kneading the dough makes the gluten stronger and stretchier.
story:
Nolan's stall at the farmers' market was really a folding table with a hand-lettered sign: FRESH BREAD, SATURDAY ONLY. He was baking dinner bread for his family tonight, and he'd convinced his mother that making a few extra loaves to sell would cover the cost of the flour. His first two loaves that morning had come out flat and dense, and Tatum, who had come to help, kept poking at one of them like it might wake up.

"They didn't rise right," Nolan said, turning a loaf over. "And I let them rise the same as always. Same yeast, same warm spot by the window." He chewed his lip. "So it has to be something I did before that." He thought back through the morning. He'd been in a hurry because the market opened at nine, so where he usually kneaded the dough for a long while, today he'd squeezed in maybe three minutes and shoved it into the bowl. That was the only thing different. His assumption had been that kneading was just mixing, and mixing took one minute, tops.

"Ten minutes," said a voice behind them. Mr. Cruz, who sold honey two tables down, was holding one of the failed loaves. "My grandmother made me knead for ten minutes, no less. The gluten, the stuff in wheat flour, forms when the flour meets water. Kneading makes it stronger and stretchier." He set the loaf down and went back to his jars, humming.

Nolan stared at the table. Stretchier. That would be like a net that could hold the air in while the bread rose, which his flat loaves plainly could not do. He couldn't see gluten, but he could test the idea. He had one batch of dough left, rising at home in a slow, lazy lump. He turned to Tatum. "Come on. We're going back to my kitchen."

In the kitchen, Nolan set the timer for the full ten minutes and pushed and folded the dough while Tatum called out the minutes like a coach. "Four! Five and a half!" The dough changed under his hands, turning from shaggy and tearable to smooth, and when he pulled a piece, it stretched into a thin window instead of snapping. He shaped it, let it rise until it domed over the bowl edge, and slid it into the oven. When the loaf came out golden and tall, the smell alone made Tatum elaborate on its greatness at length, going on about the crackling crust until Nolan laughed and covered the loaf with a towel.

They sold the second loaf at the market for the exact equivalent of what Nolan had spent on flour, which felt like a fair trade for a lesson. On the walk home, Tatum hefted the tall loaf in both hands and said, "Same time next Saturday?"

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: Charles Darwin published his theory of evolution by natural selection in the book On the Origin of Species in 1859.
story:
Luke knelt at the edge of Miller's Pond with a bag of mixed birdseed, a pair of tweezers, a spoon, and a pair of needle-nose pliers spread out on a towel. Christophe crouched beside him, and Elody sat cross-legged on the grass, guarding the notebook.

"Explain it one more time," Christophe said, "because last night my uncle called it a theory and laughed."

"Everything in science is called a theory," Elody said. "That's not an insult."

Luke poured a stripe of seed along a flat rock, then scattered a handful of tiny gravel-sized seeds in the muddy patch near the cattails. "Big seeds here, tiny seeds there," he said. "Each tool is a beak. Tweezers are a thin beak, pliers are a heavy one. We time which beak can pick up what, and where." He had gotten the idea on Saturday, browsing the dusty second-hand shop with his grandpa, who was famously frugal and refused to pay full price for anything, including paperbacks. On a shelf between cookbooks, Luke had found a battered copy of On the Origin of Species. The bookseller had looked at the faded title page and told him Darwin published it in 1859. Luke had checked the date twice, because it seemed impossible that someone had written all this before cars, before planes, before anyone knew what DNA was.

Christophe wanted the tweezers, so Luke took the pliers and Elody held the stopwatch. On the big seeds, the pliers cracked and gathered them fast, while Christophe's tweezers slipped and bent. On the tiny seeds near the mud, the roles flipped. The tweezers darted and plucked; the pliers fumbled like oven mitts. Christophe frowned at his bent tweezers, then at the pond, where two ducks were sieving algae with flat, wide bills. "So the birds on different islands ended up with different beaks because each island had different food," he said slowly, "and the birds whose beaks matched the food had more chicks."

"Nobody watched it happen," Luke said. "That's what took me a while. It's like diagnosing why the pond smells in August. You can't see the cause, so you look at clues and test them. Darwin couldn't watch the finches change either. He looked at what was there and worked backward." Elody scribbled the times in the notebook and announced that tweezers beat pliers on small seeds by nine seconds.

Christophe had said that morning that the project sounded boring, and he'd only come because Elody had promised him the leftover snacks. Now he was asking whether they could add sunflower seeds, and whether a spoon might stand in for a duck's bill. He still hadn't said he was wrong about the theory, exactly, but he was squinting at the ducks with his chin in his hand. "If we win the fair," he said, "I get to be the one who presents it. You two are terrible ambassadors. You explain too much." Elody snapped the notebook shut and tossed him the last bag of sunflower seeds. "Deal," she said. "Now pick up your beak and get to work."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: In belly breathing, also called diaphragmatic breathing, the belly rises as you breathe in instead of the shoulders lifting, which lets the lungs fill more deeply.
story:
Justin had a problem, and the problem was Thursday. Every Thursday evening, his stomach knotted up before Friday's math quiz, and last week he had been so tired he put his name on the wrong paper. He wanted to figure out what was going wrong, so he invited Elias over to help him investigate.

"It's like something sneaks up on you," Elias said, dropping his backpack on the kitchen floor. "Something sinister. You can't see it, but you can see what it does."

"Like a carnivore stalking prey," Justin said, and Elias laughed, because in science they had just learned that predators hide before they strike. "But stress isn't a carnivore. It doesn't eat you."

"It kind of does," Elias said. "It eats your sleep." He pointed at Justin, who was standing at the counter shredding a napkin into little strips without noticing. "See, that's a sign. You're doing that right now."

Justin looked down at the shredded napkin and stopped. He tried to isolate each clue, the way they did in class: the napkin, the knot in his stomach, the way he had stared at the ceiling until midnight on Wednesday. "So the pattern is, I get stressed, then I can't sleep, then I'm worse on the quiz."

"A hidden cause," Elias agreed. "My cousin taught me something for that. Put a hand on your stomach and breathe."

They both stood there in the kitchen with their hands on their bellies, which felt silly, but Justin kept going. He breathed in and watched Elias's shoulders climb up toward his ears.

"Yours are lifting," Justin said.

"Wait, yours aren't. Your hand is moving."

Justin looked down. His belly was pushing out under his hand, rising like a small balloon, while his shoulders stayed still. When Elias breathed in, only his shoulders went up, and his hand didn't move at all.

"That's the difference," Justin said slowly. "The belly rises when I breathe in, instead of the shoulders lifting. Yours is backwards from mine."

"My cousin called it diaphragmatic breathing," Elias said. "Belly breathing. She said the lungs fill more deeply that way."

They tested it. Justin lay flat on the kitchen floor with a book balanced on his stomach, and every slow breath lifted the book toward the ceiling. Elias tried it and his book just sat there until he copied the belly part. After five minutes, the knot in Justin's stomach had loosened, like a fist unclenching.

They built a routine right there. Justin got a marker and wrote on a paper towel: quiz review done by eight, phone in the kitchen drawer, ten slow belly breaths, lights out at nine-thirty. He taped it to the refrigerator, right beside the grocery list, where he couldn't miss it.

Thursday night, he lay in bed with his hand on his stomach and counted the rising of his belly, one, two, three, and was asleep before he reached thirty. On Friday he wrote his name on the right paper, and on the way out he found Elias by the door.

"Book on the stomach," Elias said, holding up a hand for a high five. "Same time next Thursday."
